# Trip Log Scotland

## Summary
Seven days in Scotland in late May, the Caledonian sleeper up and the sleeper back down, which turned the travel into part of the holiday rather than a chore. I boarded in London on the Friday night and woke to the Highlands sliding past the window, which is a far better way to arrive than any airport. Three nights went on Skye, the middle of the trip and the part I had planned around, and two nights in Glasgow at the end, with one night in between for the journey across. The weather was kind, mostly dry with one proper soaking, and the long northern evenings meant we were still walking at nine in the evening without a torch. I travelled light with one bag and was glad of it on the ferries and the trains. The sleeper both ways meant no wasted days at either end, and I would do it exactly the same way again. We booked the berths months ahead and the hostel on Skye not long after, which is the only reason the trip came in as cheap as it did. Packing light paid off on the ferry and the buses, and the one heavy item was a waterproof that earned its place twice over. The week was a walking holiday more than a sightseeing one, and that suited the country well.

## Highlights
The Quiraing walk on Skye was the standout, a few hours along the ridge with the ground falling away on both sides and the Trotternish landslip laid out below like something from another planet. We went early to beat the crowd and had the first mile entirely to ourselves. The Fairy Pools were busier but deserved the fuss, cold clear water in a dozen small falls, and I waded into one of the deeper pools and regretted it for about ten seconds. The Old Man of Storr was the other big walk, steeper than it looks and worth every step for the view back over the Sound. In Glasgow the Kelvingrove was the best afternoon of the city days, a proper museum with something odd in every room, and it cost nothing to get in. We ate well, a lot of seafood on the coast and a huge breakfast in Portree that kept us going all day. The drive across to Skye was its own highlight, the road rising and the islands appearing one by one. The weather held for the big walks and broke on the one day we had planned to rest anyway, which is better luck than I usually get. On the last evening in Glasgow we walked the river and ended up in a small bar with live music, a perfect close to the week. The food in Portree was better than it had any right to be for a town that size, and the seafood chowder there is worth the trip on its own. If I went back I would spend another night on Skye and one fewer in the city, though both were good.

## Costs
The whole trip came to 890 EUR, which was under what I had put aside and a pleasant surprise given how far north we went. Rail took 180 EUR, most of it the two sleeper berths, which were worth every euro for the sleep and the saved hotel nights. The hostel on Skye and the place in Glasgow together came to 300 EUR, cheap and cheerful and well placed for walking. Food and drink ran to 210 EUR, mostly simple meals and the one big breakfast, with the rest spent on ferries, buses and the odd museum donation. The balance covered the small things, a map, a couple of coffees and the tip on the last night. Nothing on the trip felt like wasted money, and I would spend the same again tomorrow. The sleeper turned out to be the best value of the lot once you count the two nights of accommodation it replaced and the day of travel it saved. I kept the receipts in an envelope and tallied them on the train home, which is how I know the figures are right rather than guessed.
